precepts.text: This is the law of the beasts, to make a difference between the unclean and the clean.
precepts.point: Verse 3 says meats are received with thanksgiving by them which believe and know the truth. The truth is the law, so the meat is sanctified by the word, not by a prayer over it.

note.label: My Temple My Choice

precepts.why:
Paul says the meat “is sanctified by the word of God and prayer.” So where were the animals sanctified to be eaten or not to be eaten? In the law.

Leviticus 11 closes: “For I am the Lord your God: ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy: neither shall ye defile yourselves with any manner of creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.” He repeats it: “ye shall therefore be holy, for I am holy.” How do you become holy? “Wherefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy”. To sanctify yourself and be holy you have to apply the law, the statutes and the commandments.

Then: “This is the law of the beasts, and of the fowl, and of every living creature that moveth in the waters, and of every creature that creepeth upon the earth: To make a difference between the unclean and the clean, and between the beast that may be eaten and the beast that may not be eaten.” This law takes in all the animals, whether they live on the earth or in the waters. That is how the word sanctifies the meat: by making a difference between what can be eaten and what cannot. Some animals are clean, some are unclean. It is basic.

The churches don't want you to learn the Old Testament, because they don't want you to be saved. “Keep my commandments, and live”. If you don't keep the law you are not going to live. John says “sin is the transgression of the law”, and “the wages of sin is death”. Eating unclean food is sin; eating pork is going to kill you, and overeating is going to kill you.

You are supposed to be the temple of God. If you keep destroying yourself with the way you eat, you are working against what the Lord says, and against the work we are all called here to do. The meat that is received with thanksgiving is the meat the law sanctified.

precepts.text: Be holy, for I am holy; do not defile yourselves with creeping things.
precepts.point: Catfish, shrimp, crab and snails are sold for aquariums as tank cleaners. Put them in murky water and they clean it by eating the filth. Shrimp are the roaches of the sea, and lobster was once fed to prisoners.

note.label: My Temple My Choice

precepts.why:
Many of our people who believe Christ is black and believe they are Israelites still struggle with Paul’s words: “For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving”. They take it to mean, just pray over it and eat whatever you want. But what makes every creature good? “And God made the beast of the earth after his kind, and cattle after their kind, and every thing that creepeth upon the earth after his kind: and God saw that it was good.” Every creature is good for its purpose. Worms are one of the best ways to prepare land for planting, but we do not eat worms. Pigs were the garbage disposal, because they eat everything. Can you pray over a human foot and eat it?

The bottom feeders have a purpose too. Catfish, loaches, shrimp and snails are sold as natural tank cleaners: they eat the uneaten food, the algae and the waste. Put crab or any bottom feeder in murky water and in a few hours it will be clear. The filter you change in a fish tank is what you eat when you eat shrimp; that is why they are called the roaches of the sea. Lobster was once fed to prisoners. And pork carries the trichinella worm, which can travel into the muscles and even the brain. If a creature’s job is to eat garbage, what will it do to you? Gout, high cholesterol, hypertension, even lost fingers and feet.

Read the verse before and the verse after. The meats are “received with thanksgiving of them which believe and know the truth”, and “thy law is the truth.” To believe is to keep the law: “He that believeth in the Lord taketh heed to the commandment; and he that trusteth in him shall fare never the worse.” And the creature “is sanctified by the word of God and prayer.” Christians never read that far.

So where does the word of God sanctify the animals? Here: “ye shall therefore sanctify yourselves, and ye shall be holy; for I am holy: neither shall ye defile yourselves with any manner of creeping thing that creepeth upon the earth.” He says it twice: “ye shall therefore be holy, for I am holy.” And how are we holy? “Wherefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy”. “This is the law of the beasts, and of the fowl, and of every living creature that moveth in the waters, and of every creature that creepeth upon the earth: To make a difference between the unclean and the clean, and between the beast that may be eaten and the beast that may not be eaten.”

“Keep my commandments, and live; and my law as the apple of thine eye.” You move like a flash when something comes at your eye; flee from sin that fast. John says, “sin is the transgression of the law”, and “the wages of sin is death”. Eating unclean food, and overeating, is destroying the temple the Most High gave you to do his work. He wants a fit army: you cannot teach discipline in the street without having it yourself, and you cannot go to camp and become a liability.

precepts.text: The law of the beasts makes a difference between the unclean and the clean, the beast that may be eaten and the beast that may not be eaten.
precepts.point: The beasts went in male and female to keep seed alive upon the face of all the earth, so that they could repopulate once the earth dried up; nature itself tells you what we should and should not be doing.

note.label: Genesis 7: The First Rain and the Flood

precepts.why:
Noah was told to take “Of every clean beast” by sevens and “of beasts that are not clean by two”. The dietary law was not yet instituted, but the Most High had already defined what was a clean beast and what was an unclean beast, all the way back in Genesis. Noah knew the difference.

Moses reiterated that law to the children of Israel: “This is the law of the beasts, and of the fowl, and of every living creature that moveth in the waters, and of every creature that creepeth upon the earth: To make a difference between the unclean and the clean, and between the beast that may be eaten and the beast that may not be eaten.” It is tied to holiness: “ye shall therefore be holy, for I am holy.”

Today this gets confused with the doctrine that says I can eat all things through Christ who strengthens me, and that is not true. The laws were instituted for us to discern between the unclean and the clean, and that difference was already known in Noah’s day.

precepts.text: The law of the beasts makes a difference between the beast that may be eaten and the beast that may not be eaten.
precepts.point: Fish is meat; all flesh is not the same flesh, but the flesh of beasts, of fishes, and of birds are all flesh. Every creature of God is good for what it was made for, and it is sanctified by the word of God, and the word that sanctifies what may be eaten is the dietary law.

note.label: Genesis 9: The Laws Before Moses and the Covenant of the Bow

precepts.why:
“Every moving thing that liveth shall be meat for you” does not mean you could eat everything. The law of what may be eaten was already understood; Noah had already taken the clean beasts by sevens and the unclean by two. Moses lays out the same thing: “This is the law of the beasts, and of the fowl, and of every living creature that moveth in the waters, and of every creature that creepeth upon the earth: To make a difference between the unclean and the clean, and between the beast that may be eaten and the beast that may not be eaten.”

There is a beast that may be eaten and a beast that may not be eaten. The doctrine that says you can pray over anything and eat it is a seducing spirit and a doctrine of devils.

precepts.text: The carcase not to be touched is spoken of the beasts as food; the command sits in the dietary law.
precepts.point: The badgers' skins settle a doctrine question. Leviticus 11 says not to touch the carcase of the unclean beast, and the badger goes on paws, yet the tabernacle had to be built with badger skins by hand. The law goes into sacrificing the unclean thing and eating it, touching it with your mouth; it is not saying a dead animal in your path cannot be moved out of the way with your hands.

note.label: Exodus 26: The Pattern Shown in the Mount

precepts.why:
The tabernacle was covered with eleven curtains of goats’ hair, “a covering for the tent of rams’ skins dyed red, and a covering above of badgers’ skins.” Yet Leviticus 11 says of the unclean beasts, “Of their flesh shall ye not eat, and their carcase shall ye not touch; they are unclean to you.”

The badgers’ skins settle the doctrine question. The tabernacle had to be built with badger skins by hand, at the Lord’s command. So the carcase not to be touched is spoken of the beasts as food; the command sits in the dietary law. The law goes into sacrificing the unclean thing and eating it, touching it with your mouth. It is not saying a dead animal in your path cannot be moved out of the way with your hands.

“And whatsoever goeth upon his paws, among all manner of beasts that go on all four, those are unclean unto you: whoso toucheth their carcase shall be unclean until the even.” The badger goes on paws, and that is what makes the badger an unclean beast.

And still the Most High commanded a covering of badgers’ skins over his own tabernacle, made by the hands of Israel. That is the proof the law of touching the carcase goes into sacrificing the unclean thing and eating it, touching it with your mouth, not into handling it with your hands.

note.label: Leviticus 11: The Dietary Law of Clean and Unclean Beasts

precepts.why:
The coney “cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof; he is unclean unto you.” The coney is the pika, a small mountain dwelling mammal that resembles its close relative the rabbit, found at heights among the highest of any mammal.

The scriptures already had it right: “The high hills are a refuge for the wild goats; and the rocks for the conies.” A rock dwelling animal of the high hills, exactly where the pika lives.

Whatever it is called, it has only the one mark, chewing the cud, and not the divided hoof. Both marks must be present, so you cannot eat coney, and the hare likewise is unclean.

“The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks.” Solomon describes the same animal as the psalm: small, feeble, and living among the rocks. That is the pika, the coney of Leviticus 11:5.

Knowing the animal settles the matter. It “cheweth the cud, but divideth not the hoof”, one mark and not the other, so it is unclean to you. Leave it alone, as with the camel, the hare and the swine.

It is sanctified by the word of God. The Most High explained everything and then summed it up: “To make a difference between the unclean and the clean, and between the beast that may be eaten and the beast that may not be eaten.” That difference is what the word of God sanctifies.

There is a beast that may be eaten and a beast that may not. The Most High did not change the duty of a pig, a hawk or a vulture. The unclean animals are the scavengers, the garbage disposal of the earth, made to filter the filth, while the clean animals have a filtration system so their meat is safe. Nothing in the vision changed the nature of any animal.
